Annual Crop Land: Annual Crop Land has rectangular or polygonal field parcels with sharp, straight boundaries that reflect human-imposed geometric regularity.
Annual Crop Land shows adjacent plots with strong tonal contrast—such as bare soil next to green vegetation—creating a high-contrast mosaic pattern.
Annual Crop Land displays fine, uniform texture within each field parcel, unlike the coarse, clumpy texture of Pasture Land.
Annual Crop Land contains linear access tracks or irrigation ditches aligned precisely with field edges, forming a grid-like network.
Annual Crop Land lacks the repeated circular or oval dot patterns of tree crowns seen in Permanent Crop Land.
Annual Crop Land exhibits fields with visible bare soil patches, distinguishing it from the continuous grassy cover of Pasture Land.
Annual Crop Land features field boundaries that are more sharply defined and narrower than the diffuse, irregular edges typical of Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Annual Crop Land shows low-canopy vegetation with minimal vertical structure, contrasting with the tall, dense, dark canopy of Forest.
Annual Crop Land has parcel sizes that are typically larger and more uniform than the small, irregular patches found in Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Annual Crop Land contains straight, parallel field boundaries that form long, uninterrupted lines, unlike the sinuous or fragmented boundaries of natural vegetation.
Annual Crop Land displays a higher density of internal linear features—like furrows or drainage lines—per unit area than Permanent Crop Land.
Annual Crop Land shows seasonal variation in dominant color—such as brown or gray soil tones—unlike the consistently green hues of Pasture Land.
Annual Crop Land has field shapes that are predominantly right-angled and orthogonal, whereas Pasture Land parcels often follow topographic contours with curved boundaries.
Annual Crop Land exhibits abrupt transitions in surface texture between neighboring parcels, unlike the gradual tonal blending seen in Forest.
Annual Crop Land contains no standing water bodies or persistent wetland patterns, distinguishing it from flooded rice paddies sometimes misclassified as agricultural land.
Annual Crop Land shows minimal shadow variation within fields due to low, even vegetation height, unlike the pronounced crown shadows in Permanent Crop Land.
Annual Crop Land features field edges that align across multiple adjacent parcels, creating extended straight-line segments absent in Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Annual Crop Land has a higher proportion of non-vegetated surface area—especially during planting or harvest—than the near-complete ground cover of Pasture Land.
Annual Crop Land displays consistent parcel orientation across large areas, reflecting mechanized cultivation, unlike the haphazard alignment of natural vegetation patches.
Annual Crop Land lacks the dendritic or branching patterns of natural stream networks, instead showing linear features oriented orthogonally to dominant field axes.
Forest: Forest is dominated by dark green tones rather than the lighter green or yellowish hues typical of Herbaceous Vegetation Land or Annual Crop Land.
Forest exhibits coarse, mottled texture from overlapping tree crowns, unlike the smoother, more uniform texture of Pasture Land.
Forest shows large contiguous wooded patches exceeding several hectares in size, whereas Permanent Crop Land typically appears in smaller, regularly spaced orchard parcels.
Forest has soft, irregular natural boundaries that follow terrain contours, in contrast to the rigid geometric parcel edges common in Annual Crop Land.
Forest lacks visible internal field divisions such as plow lines or harvest striping, which are prominent in Annual Crop Land and Pasture Land.
Forest displays shadowed crown structure creating variable brightness across the canopy, unlike the even illumination often seen over low-stature Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Forest contains few or no straight-line road networks cutting through the area, whereas Permanent Crop Land frequently features orthogonal access roads.
Forest shows minimal presence of roofs or paved surfaces, distinguishing it clearly from built-up areas and also from scattered farmsteads in Pasture Land.
Forest has no regular row patterns of vegetation spacing, unlike the evenly spaced linear rows characteristic of Permanent Crop Land orchards.
Forest exhibits spatial patterns aligned with natural drainage or slope rather than the rectilinear street grids found in urban or peri-urban land uses.
Forest presents a high-density vegetation cover with near-continuous canopy closure, unlike the patchy or sparse cover often seen in degraded Pasture Land.
Forest lacks the smooth, reflective surfaces of open water bodies, which may appear within or adjacent to Herbaceous Vegetation Land or floodplain Pasture Land.
Forest shows branching, dendritic linear features consistent with natural stream channels, not the straight, engineered canals sometimes seen in irrigated Annual Crop Land.
Forest contains no visible irrigation infrastructure such as center-pivot circles or grid-aligned ditches, which distinguish many Annual Crop Land examples.
Forest has irregular canopy gaps shaped by natural disturbance or topography, not the uniform, rectangular gaps created by field access paths in Permanent Crop Land.
Forest displays muted color variation across the scene due to dominant chlorophyll absorption, unlike the brighter seasonal color shifts in deciduous Annual Crop Land during senescence.
Forest shows no evidence of recent soil disturbance like bare-earth plowing strips, which are visually salient in newly tilled Annual Crop Land.
Forest features complex vertical layering evident as texture variation and shadow depth, unlike the single-layer flatness of low-growing Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Forest contains winding, narrow linear features consistent with unpaved forest trails, not the wide, straight, gravel or asphalt roads common in Pasture Land.
Forest has no visible geometric arrangement of trees aligned to planting grids, distinguishing it from the precisely spaced monoculture plantations of Permanent Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land: Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows irregular, naturalistic patch boundaries without the straight-edged, geometric field blocks characteristic of Annual Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land displays broad, continuous areal patches rather than the narrow linear corridors typical of rivers or roads.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land exhibits soft, fine-grained grassy texture without the dark, coarse, shadowed canopy texture seen in Forest.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has green to yellow-brown dominant surface tones that shift seasonally, unlike the consistently dark green of dense Forest canopies.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks plow lines, crop rows, or segmented field geometry that clearly distinguish Annual Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land contains few or no scattered trees and no dominant woody crown pattern, unlike Forest which shows repeated, high-contrast tree crowns.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows no evenly spaced planting points, orchard grids, or vineyard striping found in Permanent Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land features open, unmanaged-looking vegetation cover without the enclosed paddocks or fence-defined subdivisions common in Pasture Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has continuous vegetation surfaces without the rectilinear urban block patterns or rooftop geometries of built environments.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land presents irregular, organic patch shapes rather than the highly regular, parallel row alignments of Permanent Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks the strong linear road networks and orthogonal street grids often embedded within Pasture Land parcels.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows no smooth, specular water surfaces or distinct river meanders that would indicate open water or riparian corridors.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land displays uniform low-height vegetation density without the vertical layering and variable shadow depth seen in Forest.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has no visible building clusters, isolated farmsteads, or infrastructure nodes commonly associated with Pasture Land management.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land exhibits diffuse, non-directional texture without the aligned directional grain of cultivated Annual Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land contains no paved surfaces, rooftops, or engineered hard surfaces that contrast sharply with natural vegetation textures.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows no evidence of irrigation ditches, center-pivot circles, or other engineered water distribution features found in some Pasture or Crop Lands.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has no repetitive, evenly spaced tree or shrub clusters that would suggest managed Permanent Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land displays gentle tonal gradients across large areas rather than the abrupt color transitions between adjacent cultivated fields in Annual Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land features naturalistic edge complexity—such as dendritic or lobate margins—unlike the sharp, angular parcel boundaries of Permanent Crop Land.
Highway or Road: Highway or Road is a narrow, elongated corridor with uniform width over long distances, unlike rivers which meander and vary in width.
Highway or Road appears as a continuous linear feature connecting intersections and branching junctions, rather than isolated or clustered building footprints.
Highway or Road exhibits straight, parallel edges with sharp angular boundaries, contrasting with the irregular, organic edges of rivers.
Highway or Road has a smooth, homogeneous surface texture with minimal internal variation, unlike the textured, heterogeneous rooftops of residential or industrial buildings.
Highway or Road shows high contrast between its gray, white, or dark surface and adjacent vegetation or bare ground, whereas herbaceous vegetation land lacks such stark tonal discontinuities.
Highway or Road forms planned geometric patterns such as grids or radial corridors, unlike the irregular scattering of residential buildings.
Highway or Road occupies a thin linear footprint rather than filling an area like residential or industrial building clusters.
Highway or Road displays engineered angular intersections at consistent orientations, unlike the curved or indistinct junctions found along riverbanks.
Highway or Road maintains consistent alignment across scene boundaries, while rivers frequently shift direction and exhibit sinuosity.
Highway or Road lacks visible water surfaces or reflective sheen, distinguishing it clearly from rivers.
Highway or Road has no internal segmentation into discrete rectangular units like building footprints, making it visually distinct from residential or industrial buildings.
Highway or Road appears as a single dominant line rather than a broad, contiguous patch like herbaceous vegetation land.
Highway or Road features sharp, high-contrast transitions between its surface and adjacent land, unlike the gradual, diffuse edges typical of herbaceous vegetation.
Highway or Road shows no evidence of rooftop geometry, solar panels, or courtyard layouts that characterize residential or industrial buildings.

Highway or Road is typically bordered by narrow strips of vegetation or development but remains itself a non-vegetated linear strip, unlike herbaceous vegetation land which is fully vegetated and area-filling.
Highway or Road presents uniform reflectance across its length, whereas rivers show variable brightness due to water depth, flow, and sun glint.
Highway or Road lacks the blocky, repetitive spatial clustering seen in residential building areas.
Highway or Road has no discernible internal texture resembling grass, shrubs, or crops, setting it apart from herbaceous vegetation land.
Highway or Road follows rigidly straight or gently curved engineered alignments, unlike the natural, winding courses of rivers.
Highway or Road exhibits consistent edge parallelism over hundreds of meters, whereas industrial building perimeters are shorter, segmented, and less uniformly aligned.
Industrial Buildings: Industrial Buildings have very large rectangular roof footprints, often arranged in clusters of warehouses or factory halls.
Industrial Buildings occupy broad paved yards, loading areas, or open storage surfaces surrounding the structures.
Industrial Buildings are spaced farther apart on larger parcels than the dense small-unit pattern of Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings dominate the scene with massive building masses rather than linear transport corridors like Highway or Road.
Industrial Buildings show extensive impervious cover in gray, white, or dark tones without the repetitive row textures of Annual Crop Land.
Industrial Buildings lack the orchard grid patterns and evenly spaced tree canopies characteristic of Permanent Crop Land.
Industrial Buildings feature sharp, regular edges and block-like structures unlike the irregular, organic shapes of natural vegetation.
Industrial Buildings exhibit rectilinear geometry across both individual buildings and their overall site layout.
Industrial Buildings display organized layouts connected by wide access roads and parking lots, not narrow residential streets.
Industrial Buildings have sparse, fragmented vegetation compared to the continuous green canopy of forested land.
Industrial Buildings contain no visible crop rows, soil exposure, or seasonal growth patterns seen in Annual Crop Land.
Industrial Buildings show dominant man-made surfaces with minimal ground-level vegetation cover relative to Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings feature clustered building arrangements with large intervening paved areas, unlike isolated farmsteads.
Industrial Buildings lack the fine-scale texture and high edge density of hedgerows or field boundaries in agricultural classes.
Industrial Buildings have uniform roof colors and materials across large contiguous sections, unlike the varied surface reflectance of cropland.
Industrial Buildings show consistent alignment of building long axes parallel to adjacent wide access roads.
Industrial Buildings contain no standing water bodies, irrigation ditches, or flooded fields present in some agricultural or wetland classes.
Industrial Buildings exhibit low vegetation density and height, with no tall trees or shrub layers typical of Permanent Crop Land.
Industrial Buildings feature high-density pavement coverage extending beyond building footprints into loading zones and storage pads.
Industrial Buildings have building footprints significantly larger than those of Residential Buildings, often exceeding 5000 square meters each.
Pasture Land: Pasture Land consists of large contiguous land parcels with clearly visible field boundaries that are irregular to moderately regular in shape.
Pasture Land displays a dominant green to yellow-brown color palette reflecting grassy vegetation at varying growth stages.
Pasture Land exhibits a fine, soft texture across the entire parcel surface, lacking the strong linear row patterns seen in Annual Crop Land.
Pasture Land shows uniform vegetation density and coverage without the seasonal bare-soil patches characteristic of Annual Crop Land.
Pasture Land features sparse or absent tree cover across most of the parcel, distinguishing it from Forest.
Pasture Land has open landscape structure with very low building density, unlike urban or mixed-use agricultural zones.
Pasture Land contains human-managed spatial organization evident in adjacent farm tracks or unpaved service roads.
Pasture Land parcels often abut paved rural roads but lack the dense road networks found in Urban Land.
Pasture Land lacks the repeated linear planting geometry—such as evenly spaced tree rows—that defines Permanent Crop Land.
Pasture Land shows more homogeneous vegetation texture than Herbaceous Vegetation Land, with fewer natural transitions or patchy edges.
Pasture Land has clearer, sharper field boundaries compared to the diffuse or ecotonal edges typical of Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Pasture Land parcels rarely contain standing water bodies or linear rivers crossing their interior, unlike Wetland or Aquaculture Land.
Pasture Land exhibits minimal evidence of plowed striping or tillage marks, unlike recently cultivated Annual Crop Land.
Pasture Land maintains consistent tonal continuity across its area, without the high-contrast geometric alternation of crop and soil seen in rotational fields.
Pasture Land lacks the dense, vertically structured canopy texture and shadow complexity associated with mature Forest.
Pasture Land shows no evidence of orchard infrastructure such as support posts, irrigation lines, or trellis shadows visible at satellite scale.
Pasture Land parcels are generally larger and less subdivided than those in Permanent Crop Land, which often features tightly packed, small-scale plots.
Pasture Land has smoother, less fragmented internal texture than Herbaceous Vegetation Land, which often displays natural clumping or wind-rippled heterogeneity.
Pasture Land contains few to no built structures within parcel interiors, contrasting sharply with the frequent barns, silos, or sheds in Mixed Farmstead Land.
Pasture Land avoids the angular, highly rectilinear parcel geometry common in intensively surveyed Annual Crop Land, favoring gentler, organic boundary curves.
Permanent Crop Land: Permanent Crop Land has large contiguous parcels with sharp, straight-edged boundaries that contrast with the irregular, fragmented edges of Forest.
Permanent Crop Land shows rectangular or elongated field shapes arranged in tightly packed, human-planned grids unlike the amorphous, organically shaped patches of Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Permanent Crop Land displays regularly spaced linear rows of woody vegetation visible as parallel dark-green stripes, distinct from the uniform green blur of Annual Crop Land.
Permanent Crop Land exhibits repeating dot-like canopy elements aligned in precise grids or lines, unlike the clumped, uneven tree distribution of Forest.
Permanent Crop Land contains internal straight farm access tracks dividing fields into geometric subunits, absent in the trackless, continuous canopy of Forest.
Permanent Crop Land features terraced plots following elevation contours with consistent step widths and straight retaining edges, unlike the smooth, unsegmented slopes of Pasture Land.
Permanent Crop Land shows alternating bands of darker vegetation and lighter bare soil or low grass between rows, contrasting with the homogeneous green texture of Pasture Land.

Permanent Crop Land has higher spectral contrast between adjacent parcels due to uniform within-parcel vegetation and sharp inter-parcel boundaries, unlike the gradual tonal transitions of Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Permanent Crop Land displays vineyard-style parallel rows with consistent spacing and orientation across entire fields, whereas Annual Crop Land lacks visible internal structure at the same scale.
Permanent Crop Land contains evenly spaced, discrete tree canopies forming a dotted texture over light-toned inter-row ground, unlike the dense, seamless canopy cover of Forest.
Permanent Crop Land shows high within-parcel texture uniformity—consistent pixel-level variation—unlike the patchy, variable texture of natural Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Permanent Crop Land has field boundaries aligned to cardinal directions or fixed azimuths across multiple adjacent parcels, unlike the haphazard alignment of boundaries in Pasture Land.
Permanent Crop Land exhibits elongated, narrow plots oriented perpendicular to slope for erosion control, differing from the broad, contour-following shapes of Annual Crop Land.
Permanent Crop Land reveals straight, thin linear gaps between planted rows that persist across the full length of the field, unlike the irregular, discontinuous gaps in Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Permanent Crop Land displays high-density, regularly spaced canopy elements with minimal overlap, creating a perforated green pattern unlike the solid green mass of Forest.
Permanent Crop Land shows consistent row width and spacing across hundreds of meters, whereas Annual Crop Land exhibits uniform cover without measurable internal periodicity.
Permanent Crop Land contains orthogonal grid patterns formed by intersecting access roads and planting rows, absent in the radial or winding track patterns of Pasture Land.

Permanent Crop Land has sharp tonal transitions between adjacent fields due to identical crop types and management, unlike the gradual color blending seen at boundaries between Forest and Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Permanent Crop Land features parallel rows with consistent spectral signature intensity and spacing, unlike the variable brightness and irregular spacing of scattered trees in open Forest.
Permanent Crop Land displays uniformly sized, circular or oval canopy crowns arranged in rigid lattice formation, contrasting with the irregular crown sizes and random placement in Forest.
Residential Buildings: Residential Buildings are characterized by clusters of small to medium rectangular roof footprints arranged in tight proximity, unlike the few large, isolated building blocks typical of Industrial Buildings.

Residential Buildings exhibit a fine-grained spatial texture with alternating patches of roofs, small yards, and scattered trees, contrasting with the coarse, uniform expanse of open paved lots in Industrial Buildings.

Residential Buildings show a dense, hierarchical network of narrow streets and driveways forming cul-de-sacs and grid-like neighborhood blocks, whereas Highway or Road appears as a single dominant linear corridor with minimal branching.

Residential Buildings display a high proportion of impervious surfaces in muted tones—gray, white, and dark brown roofs alongside light-gray paved driveways—distinct from the uniform green-brown tonality of Annual Crop Land.

Residential Buildings feature parcelized land divisions with regular, rectilinear boundaries aligned to street grids, unlike the irregular, organic edges often seen along water bodies or natural vegetation.

Residential Buildings contain numerous small, discrete roof shapes—mostly rectangles and L-shapes—with sharp corners and consistent orientation, differing from the massive, monolithic roof forms of Industrial Buildings.

Residential Buildings have low building height variation visible as subtle tonal differences across roofs, in contrast to the pronounced shadowed vertical relief sometimes seen in tall Industrial Buildings.
Residential Buildings occupy moderate-sized patches typically ranging from 0.1 to 2 km², smaller and more fragmented than the expansive, contiguous tracts of Annual Crop Land.

Residential Buildings show frequent interruptions in built-up coverage by small, irregularly shaped vegetated areas—often tree canopies over lawns—unlike the broad, uninterrupted canopy of Permanent Crop Land.
Residential Buildings lack long, parallel, evenly spaced linear features characteristic of Annual Crop Land rows, instead showing short, intersecting road segments at varied angles.
Residential Buildings display a balanced mix of built and vegetated surface area within each patch, whereas Highway or Road is dominated by a single continuous paved strip with negligible vegetation.

Residential Buildings feature right-angled intersections and orthogonal street layouts that form closed blocks, unlike the curvilinear or radial patterns occasionally found in some Industrial Building complexes.
Residential Buildings contain no large, unbroken paved surfaces exceeding 50 m in width, distinguishing them clearly from the wide, straight, uninterrupted lanes of Highway or Road.

Residential Buildings show high edge density due to numerous small property boundaries and driveways, producing a jagged perimeter outline compared to the smooth, elongated boundary of Highway or Road.

Residential Buildings have rooftops predominantly oriented east-west or north-south in alignment with street grids, while Industrial Buildings often show arbitrary or clustered orientations due to functional layout constraints.

Residential Buildings include visible setbacks between structures and roads—evident as narrow strips of grass or pavement—absent in the direct, wall-to-pavement transitions common in Industrial Buildings.

Residential Buildings exhibit low spectral uniformity across the patch, with rapid pixel-level changes between roof, soil, grass, and tree canopy, unlike the spectrally homogeneous expanses of Permanent Crop Land.

Residential Buildings lack the large, geometrically perfect rectangles of field-scale agriculture seen in Annual Crop Land, instead showing irregularly sized building parcels bounded by winding or angled property lines.

Residential Buildings contain minimal exposed bare soil outside driveways and foundations, contrasting with the extensive tilled, light-brown soil patches common in Annual Crop Land during planting seasons.

Residential Buildings avoid long, straight, unbroken waterways or shorelines cutting through the patch; when water is present, it appears as small ponds or narrow drainage ditches embedded within the neighborhood fabric.
River: River is a long, narrow, elongated linear feature that traverses the scene rather than forming a broad enclosed basin like a lake or sea.
River appears as a sinuous or branching channel with visible bends and tributary-like connections, unlike the straight, engineered margins of highways or roads.
River has irregular natural banks that follow topographic contours, in contrast to the sharp, uniformly straight edges of highways or roads.
River width varies gradually along its course, whereas highways and roads maintain relatively uniform width over short distances.
River surfaces exhibit smooth or fine-textured appearance compared to the coarse, dense canopy texture of forests.
River displays darker blue, dark green, or gray tones depending on water depth and sediment, distinct from the warmer browns and tans of dry soil or paved roads.
River boundaries are sharply contrasted against adjacent land cover, unlike the diffuse or gradual transitions often seen at forest edges.
River lacks internal roof patterns, crop rows, or built-up grid structures that appear in urban or agricultural areas.
River forms continuous connected shapes rather than many small discrete objects like ponds or isolated water bodies.
River is commonly bordered by thin strips of riparian vegetation that closely follow the channel’s meanders, unlike the abrupt, right-angled transitions between road and shoulder.
River shows no lane markings, painted lines, or median dividers that characterize highways and roads.
River exhibits subtle variations in tone along its length due to changing depth or sediment load, unlike the spectrally uniform surface of paved roads.
River occupies a topographically low position in the landscape, often aligned with valleys, whereas highways frequently traverse ridges or cut across slopes.
River has no geometric regularity in its path—its curvature is organic and variable—unlike the rectilinear or gently curved alignments of planned roads.
River surfaces lack the specular highlights and consistent reflectance of sunlit sea surfaces under uniform illumination.
River appears as a single dominant linear corridor without parallel companion lines, unlike dual-carriageway highways or multi-lane roads.
River channels often split into braided or anastomosing strands in wider sections, unlike the fixed, non-branching geometry of roads.
River is typically flanked by floodplain land that mirrors its sinuosity, whereas roadside development tends to be patchy and orthogonal to the road axis.
River shows no evidence of embankments, retaining walls, or engineered culverts visible as linear hard-edged features alongside its banks.

River maintains visual continuity across varied land covers—crossing forests, fields, and urban fringes—whereas roads often terminate or change alignment abruptly at jurisdictional or terrain boundaries.
Sea or Lake: Sea or Lake is a broad contiguous water expanse occupying a large area rather than a narrow elongated channel.
Sea or Lake has a compact, rounded, lobed, or irregular basin or coastal shape instead of a thin meandering linear form.
Sea or Lake exhibits a much greater width-to-length ratio than a river.
Sea or Lake shows an interior surface largely uninterrupted by bars, banks, or frequent crossings that segment the feature.
Sea or Lake displays a smooth or nearly textureless surface compared with vegetated or built-up areas.
Sea or Lake has a generally uniform dark blue, blue-green, or gray tone across broad areas.
Sea or Lake lacks field boundaries within its surface unlike Herbaceous Vegetation Land or Pasture Land.
Sea or Lake lacks building footprints within its surface unlike built-up land classes.
Sea or Lake lacks road grid patterns within its surface unlike urban or agricultural land.
Sea or Lake features edges defined by shorelines or banks that sharply separate water from land.
Sea or Lake contains specular brightness or sun-glint patches on parts of its surface.
Sea or Lake occupies a wide open-water area enclosed or bordered by shoreline rather than confined between parallel banks.
Sea or Lake shows no visible linear river channels crossing or dividing its interior.
Sea or Lake has no discernible vegetation texture or density within its surface area.
Sea or Lake presents no evidence of herbaceous canopy cover or patchy green tones characteristic of Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Sea or Lake contains no grazing patterns, fencing lines, or pasture-like segmentation seen in Pasture Land.
Sea or Lake shows no alignment of linear features such as hedgerows or crop rows typical of agricultural land.
Sea or Lake has no clustered or dispersed building arrangements that would indicate human settlement.
Sea or Lake exhibits no evidence of soil exposure, plowed furrows, or bare-earth patterns common in cultivated land.
Sea or Lake displays no branching or tributary structures characteristic of river networks.
